utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask the witness to stand and to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Vidovic, I assume. I gather that the order of witnesses today is Mr. Vidovic, Mr. Covic, and then Mrs. Bralo. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we can start with Mr. Vidovic. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself. Tell us your name, where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Josip Vidovic. I was born on the 7th of November, 1944, in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And who are you living with?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm living with my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Are you physically in good condition or not? Were you able-bodied in 1993? Were you fit to serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I am disabled because I had surgery on my spine, spinal surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What is your wife doing today?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My wife is a teacher in the school in Ahmici where she is still working.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So she's working in Ahmici to this day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now she's working in Santici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What is her ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What is her name?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Her name is Fikreta Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Will you please tell us whether you were ever mobilised before or after the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The screens are not working, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Your screen?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic's is not working, and the booths are not working, the screens in the booths are not working, the interpreter booths, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we will try to fix this matter. Counsel Radovic, do you mind if we go on? Because some screens are working, and in a few minutes -- no? All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So I can continue, Mr. President, can I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand Counsel Radovic is opposing. No? We can continue? Thank you. All right. So in matter of a few minutes, your screen will be working. Thank you, Counsel Radovic. Counsel Susak, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, were you ever mobilised into the Croatian army, or rather the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: For reasons of health?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you keep watch duty in your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you didn't?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Would you tell us exactly where your house is situated?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is in Santici, number 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Is it along the road?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 20 metres from the road, from the Vitez/Busovaca road, on the northern side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Whose houses are situated on the southern side of the road? Are Nazif, Asim, and Ramiz Ahmic's houses close by?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ramiz's house is 30 metres from the road, Nazif's 5, and Asim's 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So those three houses are on the other side of the road; that is, on the southern side of the road?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the southern side, across the road from mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you were on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Split on the 12th and 13th. I was waiting for my daughter, who was in Paris with her child, so I went to fetch them in Split. I left Split on the 14th, and there was a jam at Sebesce in the night from the 14th to the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So tell us when you reached Santici.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I reached Santici around 3.30 on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So we want to know what happened next. What did you do on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I arrived home. As it was raining, I left my daughter and grandchild at home. The next day, I went to fetch her at school, at a quarter to 4.00, and brought her home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And until when did you stay home?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the evening, as friends and relatives came over, and the last guests left about 1.00 a.m. on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So until very late at night, you had this party, and when did you go to bed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went to bed after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Who else was in your house when you went to bed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Myself, my wife, two children, and a grandchild.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So we come to the day of the 16th of April, 1993. Tell us, what do you know about that day, the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1993, about five-something, I don't know exactly, my wife woke me up. She said she heard noise around the house and that I should go and look around. I got dressed and went out. I went to the next-door house, Vinko Vidovic's house, which is only a few metres away from mine. I saw people in front of his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What do you mean, "people"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were women, children, on the road. I went up to see whether anything had happened, as these are all relatives of mine. Then they told me that I had to wake mine up, to get ready to go into a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you take your family to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was hard for me to persuade them, but I had to. I took them as far as the road, and I went with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What happened with you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you stayed at home on the 16th after sending the family off to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Will you tell us, in the morning, did you hear where the gunfire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is very difficult to tell, especially when you're inside. It seems to you that it's coming from any side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: If you had known that a war would break out, would you have brought your daughter and grandchild from Paris to Santici?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't have brought her not only to Santici, I wouldn't have brought her to that country at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, did you see soldiers in your house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. In the house?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I mean in the yard. Or let me rephrase it. Did you see anyone in your garden on the 16th? Did a person come to your house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I tell you in order?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, do.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As I send them off to the shelter, I came back home. There was gunfire. When it subsided a little around 8.00, my nephew, Vinko Vidovic, was with me in the house. Then we went outside to see his house and his mother, how they were. Vinko went to his mother's house. I circled around the house, and when I came back into the house, I found women and children inside. The wife of Sakib Pezer with her children, Sefik Pezer's wife with children, Sefik Pezer's daughter-in-law with children. There were three women and some five or six with children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were they all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Will you give us a whole sentence in your answer?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And then what did you do when you saw them in your house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did I do? I asked them, "How come?" And they said their houses were on fire. They didn't know where they should go, so they had come to my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was it dangerous for them to be in your house, since your house was right next to the road?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I told them that it was dangerous there, that I had sent my family away, that they too should go, but it was very hard to convince them to leave and go anywhere. After some persuading, about an hour or two, I sent Vinko Vidovic up to the road to see where the others were, which shelter they were in. He found a boy, Nenad Kristo, a young man of 16, as he was in the shelter too, and he told him that they were all in Slavko Vrebac's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So I suggested that they go there as well, because they would be safer there, as we were right next to the road. I wasn't sure as regards my own safety, but they wouldn't go. Finally they agreed, but they wanted someone to take them there, so I sent Vinko to call Nenad Kristo to come over and take them there because he knew the safest route to the shelter. About 1.00, maybe half past 1.00, Nenad Kristo came, and they left with him in the direction of the Vrebac house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Slavko Vrebac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And you were still in your own house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stayed at home. Shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, you tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: About half past 1.00, my sister's son came over, Josip Covic, to see how I was and what the situation was like, and then he told me, when he had seen that these others had left for the shelter, then he said that our neighbours across the way were still in their houses, that they hadn't reached the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, for the benefit of Their Honours, will you tell us the names of the people you are referring to? Whose houses were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The house of Ramiz, Nazif and Asim Ahmic's houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: The houses across the road from yours?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: When he told you that, what did you do, the two of you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We discussed how we should go there, because we didn't dare move around much, and so I asked Josip to go back to his own house to enquire whether it was safe to move around, so that we could go and see how they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Forgive me, I have to interrupt you. You said that they should go and look for someone who would make it possible for you to go across the road to the Ahmici house. What did you mean, "Somebody"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I meant somebody who was well aware of the situation and where and who could move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: About 15 or 20 minutes later, maybe half an hour later, Josip Covic came with his brother Zoran Covic and Slavko Rajkovic to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So they were in your yard?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Then what was the conversation that you had?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Rajkovic asked us who knew those neighbours exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Zoran Covic and Josip Covic had brought him over and told him what the situation was, and then they asked you who knew those people well and who they were?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So I said I knew all of them, so myself, Rajkovic and Josip, we followed him in line, one by one, and we reached Ramiz Ahmic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, when the three of you went to the Ahmici houses, who went to fetch the Ramiz family? Was it only you and Josip Covic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Rajkovic had a different role.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I and Josip Covic went with Slavko to the Ramiz house, as this was a person who was allowed to move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Rajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So when you reached those houses, whose house did you reach first?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The house of Ramiz Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When we reached the house, we saw two soldiers with masks, and Slavko Rajkovic went up to him. They talked. They approached the stable door and the garage. They opened the door, and the women and children came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: When the women and children came out, where did they go? Did anyone go with them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the women and children came out, because we knew each other very well, Sena Ahmic and Sena's daughter, Elma, came up to me and said, "Josip, what is this?" I said I didn't know myself. Sena said something to me, I didn't quite understand. I just understood Elma saying there was soldiers in masks, and she was pointing to her house. I'm not quite sure what it was she was saying. She was probably referring to soldiers with masks who had come to their house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Elma Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, what else did Elma say to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She said that they were all -- all had masks, masked faces or painted faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Let me read to you a part of Elma's statement to see whether it coincides with yours. She says the following: "On the 16th of April, 1993, I got up at 5.00 to study for school. I looked through the window, and I saw the house of (redacted) on fire. Five minutes later, about 20 soldiers in camouflage uniforms came to our yard and started shooting at our house." (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak, I mean you were reading a statement by Elma Ahmic, who has never testified, to the best of our knowledge. Is it a statement you received from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I received the statement from the Prosecution, and I am surprised, but the Prosecution does not object because the statement was given on the 28th of January, 1995. It was written by the investigator of the Prosecution, and it was disclosed to us. In view of the fact that statements of other witnesses were written after the indictment was confirmed by the Tribunal, it seems to me logical to be able to read a part of this statement in order to verify the statement of this witness and to contribute to the establishment of justice, anyway. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak, since this witness has not testified, we feel that you may summarise her statement, but you should not put it in evidence and it should not be put on the record. So can you simply summarise that statement and ask Mr. Vidovic to comment on that statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I only have another three or four words to read from this statement. When I was saying about Elma Ahmic's statement, it was in quotation marks and I am continuing. "They all had painted faces."

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, what Elma told you, does that coincide with the statement I have just read?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. That is what she wanted to say to me, because she was pointing with her hand and saying "painted mask." That is probably what she meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did she tell you they had paint on their faces?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So she told you that they all had paint on their faces. When you saw these two men in front of the Ahmic house, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They had camouflage black uniforms and paint on their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I mean some coloured stuff on their face.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And how was Slavko Rajkovic dressed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Rajkovic was also wearing a camouflage uniform, and he had some lines on his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So we've come to the point when you said that these Muslims came out. Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the stable, where they were released by the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Whose stable was it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ramiz Ahmic's. And when they came out, I saw Asim Ahmic's wife and children, so I proposed to Josip that the two of us go to see where the other women and children were. So for safety's sake, we went behind the stable where they had been locked up, and behind the stable we came across four bodies, four corpses. Among the four, I recognised three. One was that of Ramiz Ahmic; the second, his son, Nazif Ahmic; and the third body was Nazif's son. I think his name was Amir Ahmic. I did not recognise the fourth body because the face was turned towards the ground. Then we went on to Nazif Ahmic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, I have to interrupt you again. You said "we"; what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I mean myself and Josip Covic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So can it be said that you and Josip Covic went to fetch the Muslims, whereas Slavko Rajkovic had a different role? At your request, of course. Tell us a little about that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at our request, that we should find somebody who could guarantee our safety -- not safety, but allow us freedom of movement. That person was Slavko Rajkovic. So Slavko, myself, and Josip Covic went to Ramiz Ahmic's house, and after that I and Josip Covic went to Hasim Ahmic's house to see where his wife and children were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And then what?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From there, after seeing the bodies, we passed under Nazif's house, and there I didn't feel well any more. I almost fainted. I told Josip to go and check, and three or five minutes later I saw Josip coming back with a woman and children and going towards the road up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Vidovic. I will show you a sketch, and I shall be asking you some questions in connection with that sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, I should like to show the sketch to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the interpreters' monitors are not working, and it is rather difficult for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D32/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, have you got this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you adjust this sketch so that you can see it well and tell us where Ramiz Ahmic's stable is, his summer kitchen, and his house.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The stable --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, would you mark the house with "A," put a big letter "A" in the middle where the house is, and then mark the summer kitchen with a capital "B," and now you can tell us where the stable is and mark it with "C." Could you please put two "Xs" where the soldiers were -- or the persons; I don't know whether they were soldiers or not.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Very well. Could you show us where the door and windows of the stables were, if there were any?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You just said that when Slavko Rajkovic brought you and Josip Covic there -- could you mark the direction from which you arrived with an arrow?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Very well. Would you please tell us where you found the four corpses, and mark that place with small circles.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Among those persons, was Amir Ahmic, who was a young boy, one of them? Was he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you mark where he was with the number "1."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well (witness marks).

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you tell us, whose house is the next house to the left?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the house of Nazif Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Would you please write "Nazif" where that house is.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that you had gone to Asim Ahmic's house; it can't be seen on this sketch, but would you draw an arrow to show us the direction in which you went.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then I went as far as this place (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you stayed here?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And Josip Covic? So who took Asim Ahmic's wife and children out of their house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Josip Covic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And where did you meet later?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He took them to the road behind the hedge, and they went toward the shelter, and I crossed the road and went on to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have completed this part of my examination concerning the houses, but I would like to show the witness an aerial photograph because there is a situation which the other witnesses did not mark the houses at the end of the road, especially on the north side.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit D33/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, can you see this aerial photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. President. While these maps are being shown and sketches, we see absolutely nothing, so we are unable to follow this part of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I do appreciate your predicament. I understand this technical problem can be sorted out only during the coffee break, so we have to wait until 10.30, or if you prefer we can adjourn now and, assuming that the technicians can sort out this technical problem -- (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: It's arrived, it's arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: We may continue, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, could you please show the Travnik-Busovaca road and put "Travnik" on one end, on the white part, "Travnik" and "Busovaca" on the other end?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Would you please indicate your house here? You can put a circle around it. Would you mark it with number "1"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What is the upper part or the northern part from the road? What is there? Could you draw a line and an arrow to say this is the northern part? You've gone too far up. Just from the road.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you draw a line from the road toward the north?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So that is the north. Put an arrow there.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So that's north. What is south of the road?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: South (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Very well. Would you now put numbers or letters to indicate the houses of Ramiz Ahmic, Asim Ahmic and Nazif Ahmic? With letters, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "A", "B", and "C", so Ramiz is "A", Nazif is "B", and Asim "C".

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the house of (redacted) (redacted) is?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How shall I mark it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And the house of Fahrudin Ahmic or Hasim Ahmic's house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So we shall not mention names. Would you put "E" next to that house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So that is north of the road?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's south.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: South, yes. You are north of the road?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where Zoran Covic's house is?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Should I circle it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, circle it and mark it with "2" or "3".

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You put "1" next to your house. Are there any other numbers?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Well, then put number "2".

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: If you can find your way, could you show us where the house of Anto Papic is? Could you adjust it so that it can be seen on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Very well. Is it the last house down?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you mark it with "F"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Witness indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Is that house quite far away from the road compared to the houses of Ramiz, Asim and Nazif?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: From Fahran Ahmic's house, can you see in the direction of (redacted)'s house? Is there a good view? Are there meadows there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When you look toward the road from (redacted) (redacted) house, is there a good view?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: We have now finished with this photograph. We shall proceed further. You mentioned two men, and you said they were wearing black uniforms and that they had paint smeared on their faces?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Where did these people go when you and Covic went to your houses?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Where did Slavko Rajkovic go, or did he stay near the houses of Ramiz Ahmic and the others?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When they left the stable, they all stayed in front of the house and we went underneath the stable, and I don't know where they went, the other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: We mentioned a Slavko Rajkovic. Do you know whether he's alive today?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, he isn't. I heard that after that intervention, an hour and a half later, that Slavko Rajkovic was killed some 800 metres away from that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You say he was killed, and was that an ambush prepared for him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but they say it was an ambush, so that somebody liquidated him or killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Since you said that you had spinal surgery and that you were not able-bodied for military service, that you did not go on patrol and that you were not mobilised in the HVO, could you say whether you were given any shares in connection with the war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was given shares too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you tell me how it came about that you did not participate in the war but you received shares?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, later when they were drawing up lists, when the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was to be a special ratio, a special percentage, and a person from the Defence came around and he said to me, "I'll put you down on the list as well for that reason," and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So did he say because you were in the area affected by war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Regardless of whether you actually took part in the war. So I repeat, you say you could not have been mobilised or go on patrol because you had had spinal surgery. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the other Defence counsel have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, my name is Michael Blaxill. I'm one of the Prosecutors in this case, and I would just like to ask you a few questions as a result of what you have said here today. You say that you awoke at around 0500 on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993, that you got your family eventually to shelter, and that at around 8.00 at your home, you encountered a number of Muslim neighbours who had come to your house. Is that a correct summary?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, but I did not take my family to the shelter but only as far as the road, and then they were left with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You then say that your nephew, Josip Covic, came over to you, and do you recall at about what time that would have been?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: About a half past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say that after that, perhaps 15 to 20 minutes later, so we're saying a quarter to 2.00 perhaps, you and Josip Covic, Zoran Covic and, I understand, if I heard you correctly, Slavko Rajkovic, all made your way in the direction of the house of Ramiz Ahmic; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What was Mr. Zoran Covic wearing at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think he was not wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What was Mr. Josip Covic, your nephew, wearing?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did either of those two gentlemen have any form of weapon in their possession?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Slavko Rajkovic I believe you described as wearing a camouflage uniform and having paint marks on his face. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say he was dressed in the way similar to the other soldiers you saw that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was dressed like the other two soldiers which we saw in front of Ramiz Ahmic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was he carrying a weapon at that time, Mr. Slavko Rajkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How long do you think it took for you to get to the house of Ramiz Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Three to four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So would I be correct in suggesting you were there at around 2.00 in the afternoon of the 16th of April, 1993; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Around 2.00, maybe ten minutes past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Subsequent to that, a number of, if I understood correctly, women and children were released from a stable building near that house. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Behind that building, you identified the dead bodies of four Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At what time do you recall leaving that scene, the house of Ramiz Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Around 20 past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At that time, did you see any other kind of military personnel in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, except the two soldiers and Rajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would it be true to say that these two soldiers were, in fact, Croat soldiers we could describe as HVO soldiers; would you say that was correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the insignia. I don't know whether they were HVO. They were probably Croats, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: On that basis, I thank you. Your Honours, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Counsel Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Vidovic, that Rajkovic, Slavko Rajkovic, was wearing black and that he was masked. Do you know that person or not? Would you recognise him now if I showed him to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't recognise that person even ten minutes afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no questions. No questions for the witness from the Court. Mr. Vidovic, thank you for testifying. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Covic. Will you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Covic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Would you please introduce yourself to the Court with your full name, when you were born, where you live.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: My name is Josip Covic. I was born in 1971. I live in Pirici and Santici, the municipality of Vitez. I'm single, and I work at the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Are you still employed at the post office?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Very well. Would you tell us whether you are familiar with the events of the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Where were you working at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I was working in the Meos centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: That is the observation and intelligence service, and that was the civil part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you were working in the centre for alerting the population?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were you an active-duty or a reserve soldier of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I was at the centre for alerting the population, so I was in the reserves, in the secretariat for national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you're saying that this centre was attached to the Defence secretariat of the Municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So how do you explain that you were in the reserves and you were working there? I thought you were on active duty.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I simply worked in that centre, because that is the civilian part. It belongs to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were you a reservist of the HVO, then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. If this centre was part of the HVO, then I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So if you were in the reserve, was Anto Bertovic your commander?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Well, then, I drew the wrong conclusions. Sorry. I considered you to be on active duty. Did you go to work every day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to work every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Then how can you say that you were in the reserves and you were active?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well, I worked actively.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you want to say that this centre was attached to the municipality and not to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you worked actively, but you were not an active soldier?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: If you had been mobilised, what would you have been? Active, an active or passive soldier of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: A passive soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But if you were mobilised, then you would have been active; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Would you tell us, where were you on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: 15th of April, 1993, I worked. I was at my work place at the centre, and then I came home around 10.00 in the evening. That was the regular shift. On the 15th, then I asked that Dragan Stojak, a regular authorisation -- that is, I had to ask for that every time I needed -- I wanted Friday to have off because of some pains which I had suffered from my childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Who was Dragan Stojak?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Stojak was the head of the intelligence centre. And if I needed something, if -- whatever, then I had to go to Dragan Stojak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was he also under the umbrella, if I can put it that way, of the defence centre in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But he was your boss?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was my boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And the control and alert centre, was it a civilian organisation or the military organisation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: It was civilian, part of the civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Of the Municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of the Municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And you said you came home in the afternoon, and you told us that Stojak let you off Thursday afternoon so that you could have a long weekend; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Where were you in the night between the 15th and 16th?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I was at home with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And where did you wake up on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were woken up by sounds of gunfire at half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And what did you do then? Did you go anywhere? Did you stay at home after you were woken up by gunfire?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: My brother and I stayed home, and my father and mother went to the next-door house where -- Mirko Jukic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So your father and mother went to Mirko Jukic's house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you go anywhere during that day? Did you leave your house at all?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, nowhere, until half past 1.00, because at half past 1.00 my father came to feed the pigs and do various chores around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So he came back from Mirko Vukic's house to your home?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And he said that Jozo Lovric and Anto Vidovic had told him that from Ramiz Ahmic's, that Ramiz Ahmic and his wife and their children and daughter-in-law were in that house and that I should go there and see that they all go to Slavko Vrebac's house, because everybody was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well, then I went to Jozo Lovric's house and to Anto Vidovic's house, and I talked to them about Ramiz's family, and then I went to Jozo Vidovic's house, because he is my uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you talked to Josip there. What was the conversation between the two of you, between you and Jozo Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well, I told Jozo Vidovic about Ramiz's family, that they should go, and that we should send them on to Slavko Vrebac's house. We agreed that I should go back home and fetch my brother Zoran and then that the three of us should go together for safety, just because of the safety, because fire came from all sides.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you please slow down so the interpreters can keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: When you talked to your brother, Josip Vidovic, where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: My brother and I -- that is, I went back to fetch my brother. I told him and explained to him what it was all about, and then my brother and I -- I mean, when we started towards Josip's house, we met Slavko Rajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, very well, so you met Slavko Rajkovic. Did you then go to Jozo Vidovic together with Slavko Rajkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And did you all get there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And what did you talk about then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: My brother Zoran told Slavko -- he was (indiscernible) kind of authority. He also told him about Ramiz's family. So we all went to Josip --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: All three of you together?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all three of us. And down there I found Drazenko Vidovic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What were they wearing? Semrin -- you said Drazenko Vidovic and Semrin?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember what they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But were they in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Will you then tell us, how did you go to Ramiz Ahmic's house, and who went there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: When Slavko Rajkovic, Zoran, that is, my brother and I reached Josip, we talked about Ramiz's family, and Slavko Rajkovic asked me if anyone knew him, was on closer terms with him, and I said that I knew him fairly well, so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You mean Jozo Vidovic said that he knew them well?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because they were next-door neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I see; because they were next-door neighbours?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then Slavko Rajkovic, Zoran, and I reached Ramiz Ahmic's house. We were in one file, one after the other. When we reached Ramiz's Ahmic's house, we found there two soldiers in black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were they soldiers, or something else? Are you sure? Are you positive they were soldiers, or just plainly two men wearing black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I think they were soldiers because they had their faces painted; they were carrying rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Right. So will you please describe how you approached them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well, we got down there. Slavko Rajkovic approached those two soldiers, talked to them about something, and then from the stable they released Ramiz Ahmic's wife, Nazif Ahmic's wife, and Rasim Ahmic's wife. There were two children, too. I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And where were they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: In the stable, in Rasim Ahmic's stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did they leave on their own, or did somebody take them away?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Josip and I, Josip and I, we went to the road together, and then we told them to go to Slavko Vrebac's house because it was safer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And were there Asim Ahmic's wife and her children?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: When we directed Nazim and Rasim and Hasim's wife and children to Josip Vrebac's, then Josip told me Asim Ahmic's wife was not there, and we should go to Asim's house to see if she was still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So who went to Asim's house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Josip and I started down the lane below Asim Ahmic's house; that is, between the summer kitchen and the stable. And below the stable we came across four bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You came across four bodies; where was that? Will you please be more precise?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: They were below -- these four bodies were below Ramiz Ahmic's stable. The first one was Ramiz Ahmic; the second one was Nazif, Ramiz's son; the third was the son of Nazif Ahmic, and the fourth one we could not identify. And then we continued to Asif's house, and Josip stayed at Asif's, that is, stayed behind at the Ramiz house, and I went to Asif's house, and I heard a child cry from the -- I heard a sound coming from the direction of the stable, so I opened the door and I told them to go towards Slavko Vrebac's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And those two other men who are uniformed, Slavko Rajkovic were there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well, right below Ramiz Ahmic's house they stayed in front of Ramiz's house, and what they did after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: There is a road there, you said, Novi Travnik/Busovaca. Is there a hedge next to the asphalt part of the road leading in the direction of Ramiz, Nazif, and Asim's house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What kind of a hedge is it? Is it something natural, naturally grown, or ... ?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was at Ramiz Ahmic's part, and at Nazif, there was this hedge, and Nazif's was sort of trimmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And so in the direction of Asim's house it was somewhat trimmed as opposed to Nazif's house, the hedge was just naturally growing?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You mentioned Slavko Rajkovic. And what was he wearing that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing a black uniform, and his face was painted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know, is he still alive today?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, he is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know, was he killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: That same day, after Ramiz's family was sent on their way, about one hour later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Would you be able to recognise him today?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know when was he killed? Was somebody else wounded at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: The day when Slavko Rajkovic was killed, Drazenko Vidovic and Ivica Semrin were wounded. It was next to Izet Karalic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: We have three annual photographs of the military police, and I will show you Slavko Rajkovic's photograph and ask you if you can recognise him or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Will the usher please help me, please, and show it first to the Court and then to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D355.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Will you please show Exhibit 355 to the witness. Let it be placed on the ELMO, and the page 376, with Slavko Rajkovic's photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know, is this that person, Slavko Rajkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What does it say? When was he killed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So on that very day, as you just told us?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And when does it say he was killed in Vitez, why does it say Vitez rather than Santici?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well, Santici is a part of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So what we have here indicated is the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you tell us, who else lived next to Ramiz, Asim and Nazif's house, or rather -- how far is Musafer Puscul's house from this house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Asim Ahmic's house is about 80 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And from Nazif or Asim Ahmic's house, can you see if somebody comes, or in other words, if a group of soldiers were coming from the direction of Musafer Puscul's house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because Asim's entrance overlooks -- faces that part of the lane which goes to Musafer Puscul's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I shall repeat. What was Slavko Rajkovic wearing?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: He had black clothes on him, a black uniform on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was his face also camouflaged?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, his face was camouflaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So he was both camouflaged and dressed in the same way as those who were in front of Ramiz Ahmic's house, those two male individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, identically. They were wearing the same kind of clothes and had their faces painted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you know that Slavko Rajkovic was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: When did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I found that out later, the day when he was killed. Then they brought him -- those two elderly men brought him over to those houses, I mean his body, and he had a patch on his left arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: A patch, insignia, what was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a patch which said "Military Police" and then "Jokers".

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: On the south side of the road, Ramiz, Nazif and Asim Ahmic and other houses, how is it that nobody came from the other side of the road to fetch Ramiz, Asim and Nazif Ahmic's families to give them shelter, and you came from the other side of the road and there were Muslims in those houses, houses that you knew about that and those others did not. How is it that you, on the other side of the road, knew where they were?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Because Jozo Lovric and Anto Vidovic, who were in the shelter, that is they first were in the shelter, in the shelter next to Slavko Vrebac's and they came out, and then there were others who were there, I mean women and children, and they said Ramiz's family was missing and so they had not come there to find shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So from the northern side of the road which was rather far from your house, you knew that there were some Muslims who had stayed behind in Ramiz and Asim Ahmics' houses, is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So they knew about that, is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you tell us, where was Slavko Rajkovic killed, next to whose house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Next to Izet Karalic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Where is that house in relation to Josip Vidovic's house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: North of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So north of the road and Josip Vidovic's house, and how far away from Josip Vidovic's house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: About, I should say, 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So they knew about Muslims who had stayed behind in Ramiz and Asim Ahmics' houses. Just one question more. When you went with Slavko Rajkovic to this stable, Ramiz Ahmic's stable, were those two male individuals with painted faces and wearing black, did Slavko Rajkovic talk to them, so would you conclude that it was Slavko Rajkovic who was ordering them to let the Muslims from Ramiz Ahmic's stable?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well yes, he approached and went to them, he talked to them, and immediately they were released. So I believe he had some authority over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you very much. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this has already become a routine of late. Other counsel have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier, would you do it now or would you rather that we make a break? Do you have many questions? More than ten minutes, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let's have a break now, the usual 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning. I'm Franck Terrier, and I represent the Prosecution in this case, and I should like to ask you several questions on the basis of your examination-in-chief. First, I should like to go back to your profession -- that is, whether you were a civilian or military -- because I did not quite understand that. You told us, if I understood you properly, that you were employed by the military, that you were in a form of military, but you were a reservist rather than an active-duty military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let me try and rephrase it. In April 1993, did you perform your job, and what was your job? Will you please tell us, as precisely as possible, what is it that was your job that April?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well, I worked for the centre for reporting, monitoring, and alerting. I worked there actively, but that was a civilian part of the Municipality of Vitez and not the military one, because it was under the national defence secretariat of the Municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So it was an organisation which was under the defence secretariat of Vitez; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is the civilian. It was under the civilian part of the Municipality of Vitez. It was the monitoring and alerting centre, so it was to alert in case of a natural disaster, too. So what I did was just sit by the telephone, and citizens would then seek information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Who were your superiors? What was the hierarchical structure?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Who issued orders to you? Who did you receive orders from in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Stojak, because he was the head of the monitoring and alerting centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And who was Anto Bertovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Anto Bertovic was the commander of the battalion, or a brigade. I don't really know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were you under the authority of Anto Bertovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you wear a uniform when you went to work?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you describe the type of the uniform that you wore to work?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: It was an ordinary camouflage uniform that I'd bought myself, but at that time children also could buy one. At that time it was quite ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were there any insignia on that particular uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, there were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you go back home, or did you stay in Vitez in the centre for monitoring and alerting? What was the usual thing that you did?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I went to work every day, and I would go home on Thursdays. That is, I would work during those several days. I would go home on Thursdays, and I always had Friday off. That was an agreement I had reached with Dragan because I had a problem with back pain, so that I always had three days off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let us now move on to the 16th of April. You told us that you were awakened by gunfire, or rather that you heard those shots when you woke up, and you told us that you stayed all day, or rather all morning; you were at home. Did I get your answer well?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was woken up by the gunfire, and I spent the morning at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And you stayed at home all morning?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What were you wearing at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Well, that camouflage uniform that I had bought.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon with you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us, if I understood you properly, that your brother Zoran was with you that morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What did your brother do at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: He was at home with me. We simply did not think there was any need for us to leave home. At the time, there were many cases of theft and things like that, and we decided we would stay at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did your brother hold a job at the time? That was my question; did he have a profession of a kind, or a job? Did he hold a job then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: My brother worked for a company called Princip, but at that particular period of time, he was also on holidays, and he was using his holidays.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Since when had he been on holidays?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I know that it was a few days before, so that -- I really don't remember. I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But as a rule, did your brother Zoran live in Ahmici, or elsewhere, at the time when he went to work?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: My brother lived in Santici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What was your brother wearing that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us, Witness, about Rajkovic, and you told us that this individual was killed that 16th of April. Could you please tell us, who did you learn this from? Who gave you this information? Please be as accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You spoke about Rajkovic, a member of the military police, Jokers, a member of Jokers, according to our testimony, who was killed on the 16th of April in Santici, Pirici, or Ahmici. Were you an eyewitness to his death?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see it with my own eyes. I was not there. I heard it from the wounded, from Drazenko Vidovic and Jovinko Samir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You also mentioned somebody called Semrin; do you remember that? Ivica Semrin.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Ivica Semrin? Yes, so I did. Yes, I did mention him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you remind us what you said? It's simply to clarify your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What is it that you told us about Ivica Semrin? Could you please repeat it? Will you please repeat just what you said a while ago?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: All I know is that he was wounded at the same place, at the same place where Slavko Rajkovic got killed. Because later on, after a certain period of time, I learned that it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, who is it that you heard it from about the wounding of Ivica Semrin? Who told you, and when, that he had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I learned that about an hour and a half after Ramiz Ahmic's family was released, because Drazenko Vidovic, who had a perforating wound in his chest, he somehow managed to get from Izret Karalic's house, and he told me that Ivica was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What was Ivica Semren?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Ivica Semrin was my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have this -- I did not show it to the Defence, because I did not think that this episode would be mentioned, because I did not think it was important. But I have here a certificate issued by the Vitez Brigade saying that Ivica Semrin, born the 29th of April, 1973, in Vitez, was a member of the HVO, Vitez Brigade, since the 8th of April, 1992; that he was wounded on the 16th of April, 1993, in Ahmici, at that time, when he was carrying out combat orders issued by the relevant authority. It also says that Zoran Ante Covic was an eyewitness to that incident, or the wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not understand it. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, I have before me a document, and of course I shall submit it to the Court, but I have an official document according to which Ivica Semren was wounded on the 6th of April, 1993, in Ahmici. At that time, there was fighting amongst the ranks of the HVO Vitez Brigade, and it says that your brother eyewitnessed this wounding, Zoran Covic eyewitnessed this wounding.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I already said it, Ivica was not a soldier. And I don't know what he was wearing, but that was not a camouflage uniform, I'm certain. Zoran Covic, was he there or was he not, I really don't know. I don't know about his movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So is it the camouflage uniform which would tell us if one is a soldier or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, will the Prosecutor, if he's referring to a document which we did not have because it has not been handed over to us, also show us this document so that we could see it? I believe there was an agreement that documents would be shown in advance. Now we are not being shown it even at the time when this document is being quoted. So will you please do something about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We know that, but Mr. Terrier has already told us twice that this document was not handed over to Defence because they did not think that this question would be raised today, so that you are quite right indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But may I also add, Mr. President, that sometimes it is very difficult to prepare cross-examination when we only get a summary such as the one which was handed over, and it says very clearly that this witness was an HVO soldier that April, it says here, defending on the battalion commanded by Anto Bertovic. Now this witness tells us quite the opposite. Sometimes it is really difficult to prepare an accurate and very specific and proper cross-examination. I'm really very sorry, but we had no opportunity to communicate to the Court and to the Defence this document, but if we may, we shall place it on the ELMO, and today naturally we should take care that it is distributed to all the parties concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I believe that if Mr. Susak asks for it, he can also suggest the re-examination of this witness, that it can be deferred until tomorrow so that they can read this document very carefully, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should like indeed to have this right and perhaps tomorrow come back and re-examine the witness as to this particular incident, and I believe it will be very brief. Will the Chamber please allow me to meet with the witness and talk to him about this document? (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. All right, you may talk to the witness about this document this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be 369.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If my learned friends from the Defence want also to have the version in the B/C/S to be placed on the ELMO, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASESSE
utterances.text: But are you going to ask other questions about this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: All I want is to get a reaction from the witness. That is all that I'm asking for. I'm not going into this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness Covic, doesn't this document say that Ivica Semren was an HVO soldier, a member of the Vitez Brigade, and that he was in action under the orders of his superiors on the 16th of April, and it was as he was engaged in combat that he was wounded; is that not what this document says?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I said already that a camouflage uniform -- that when a soldier -- that he must wear army clothes or, rather, camouflage clothes. As far as I know, Ivica Semren was not wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So does that mean it is the uniform which makes a soldier a military?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But you had a uniform too?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you were a military if you --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I was not. No, no, I was not a military. I did not have any insignia, and I said that I had bought those clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But how can we explain, then, that your uncle, who testified before you, Josip Vidovic, said, when asked during the cross-examination, I believe the 26th line of the transcript, that you were wearing civilian clothes? How could he make such a mistake?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean about the civilian force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I shall move on to another question. Could you please tell us what happened to you after the 16th of April? What did you do after the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1993, Slavko Papic came to my home and asked me to go to the Pirici area, up there, and I resisted it because I had trouble with my back. But at that time, it simply did not help, so I went to the Pirici area. And there, in the afternoon, I was wounded, so I was up there. Because I had severe pain because I had been on the move all day, I started home. It was then that I was wounded by a shell. I wish I had stayed up there at the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said that you were wounded that 16th of April, '93, that 16th of April; is that it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: No, not on the 16th of April. On the 17th of April, in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What were you doing at the time when you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: Because the wound was not so bad, I got down to the village and there were already some vehicles there, and they took me to Busovaca, that is, to the outpatient clinic in Busovaca. The next morning, then they took me home, so that the rest of the time I was at home and I received treatment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, but my question is what were you doing at the time of your wounding?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I remind the witness that he has solemnly declared that he would tell the truth, and not telling the truth entails very grave consequences. The question was very simple. Would you please ask the same question once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us you were wounded on the 17th of April, 1993. All I'm asking you is to tell us something about the circumstances of your wounding and what were you in the process of doing at that moment? Is that question clear? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC
utterances.text: So I was in the area of Pirici. Up there, there were two or three men more up there with me. However, when I returned -- so, no, after I started back home because I could not stand the pain anymore, so I was on my way home, and it was as I started for home that I was wounded by that shell.
